STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Cal Water implemented leakage recovery pilots evaluating the effectiveness of satellite and manual acoustic leak detection. The pilots were implemented in 4 systems with varying characteristics and geographic location. In addition, Cal Water conducted a detailed investigation of repair data to calculate reported leakage volume and calculated the optimal leak detection survey frequency per the AWWA Manual M36 methodology. They also developed a master production meter inventory to document and help track production meter data across various databases.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Cal Water conducted training on production data reporting, including the development of reference videos and documents to improve the data collection, management, and quality control of production data. They also developed a production database to digitally archive approved monthly production data across all districts in a centralized database. In addition, Cal Water has developed tools to allow for more frequent water loss tracking, including a Tableau visualization of monthly production and consumption data as well as quarterly water loss pulse checks. These tools allow Cal Water to flag potentially unrealistic water audit inputs and/or results for further investigation.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Dublin San Ramon Services District (DSRSD) converted its customer billing system from EDEN accounting/billing software to Tyler Technologies Munis in August 2024. The new software has better functionality to identify and verify inactive meters, which was not readily available in the older system.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: DSRSD conducted a pilot study on leak detection technologies to identify their effectiveness for PVC and Asbestos Cement pipes, the main pipe types in the DSRSD service area. Two sensors, PermaNET and FIDO AI, were evaluated. The study results showed no leaks in the two pilot areas, consistent with DSRSD's historically low non-revenue water levels. The study also showed that neither leak sensor can economically detect leaks in PVC or Asbestos Cement pipes. DSRSD plans to continue monitoring the trend of the district's real loss (currently, DSRSD meets its water loss standard) in the next few years and develop a leak detection survey program that is cost-beneficial to DSRSD customers.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Cal Water implemented leakage recovery pilots evaluating the effectiveness of satellite and manual acoustic leak detection. The pilots were implemented in 4 systems with varying characteristics and geographic location. In addition, Cal Water conducted a detailed investigation of repair data to calculate reported leakage volume and calculated the optimal leak detection survey frequency per the AWWA Manual M36 methodology. They also developed a master production meter inventory to document and help track production meter data across various databases.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Cal Water conducted training on production data reporting, including the development of reference videos and documents to improve the data collection, management, and quality control of production data. They also developed a production database to digitally archive approved monthly production data across all districts in a centralized database. In addition, Cal Water has developed tools to allow for more frequent water loss tracking, including a Tableau visualization of monthly production and consumption data as well as quarterly water loss pulse checks. These tools allow Cal Water to flag potentially unrealistic water audit inputs and/or results for further investigation.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: To support proactive leak detection, Cal Water designed a Leakage Recovery Pilot Plan to evaluate various leak detection technologies, including: Manual Acoustic Leak Detection Survey; Satellite & Aerial Imagery Analysis, Acoustic Logger Installation, and District Metered Area Monitoring

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: The City, in collaboration with Westland's Water District, identified an issue with the effluent water meter that measures water delivered to the City. To address this, Westland's Water District is rescaling the meter to ensure accurate readings. Once the issue is resolved, future audits will utilize the Coalinga Water Treatment Plant's effluent meter to measure water volume from the City's own sources rather than classifying it as imported water.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: The City is actively pursuing grant funding to replace 3,288 existing customer meters, many of which are aging touchpad models that require manual readings, some dating back over 30 years. Upon securing funding, the City will proceed with purchasing new metering equipment and issuing requests for proposals to hire a contractor for installation.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: The City began planning for the replacement of outdated customer meters by assessing available funding options and researching appropriate meter technology. Initial steps were taken to apply for grant funding to support this project. Additionally, preliminary discussions were held regarding long-term solutions for improving metering accuracy and reducing data discrepancies between the City's Surface Water Treatment Plant and the Westland's Water District effluent meters.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Future audits will rely on the Water Treatment Plant's effluent meter to measure volume from the City's own sources instead of categorizing it as imported water. Additionally, the City will begin efforts to improve water usage tracking by implementing measures to account for water used by the Public Works Department and the Fire Department during fire hydrant flushing activities. The City will also begin replacing the outdated touchpad meters with Badger Beacon meters.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Westland's Water District rescaled its effluent water meter, which measures water delivered to the City. The City had been addressing discrepancies between this meter and the effluent meter at the Surface Water Treatment Plant for several years.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: The City secured grant funding for the replacement of 3,288 existing customer meters. These meters include aging touchpad meters, some over 30 years old, which require manual readings. These outdated meters will be upgraded to Badger Beacon meters, which utilize a cellular network for continuous data collection, complementing the 740 already in use. Installation is set to begin in FY 2024-25, with full conversion expected to be completed by FY 2025-26.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: In FY 2025-26, the City will continue replacing the remaining customer meters until full conversion to cellular read technology is achieved. Upon completion, the City will focus on refining data management procedures and utilizing AMI analytics to monitor both apparent and real losses. Insights gained from this data will guide future water loss control efforts and infrastructure investments. In addition, for subsequent audits, the City will begin using the Water Treatment Plant's effluent meter to quantify production from the City's own sources, rather than categorizing it as imported water.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: During FY 2024-25, the City replaced approximately 2,100 customer meters with cellular read meters, representing a significant step toward full system modernization. These meters enhance data collection frequency, improve leak detection, and provide more accurate measurement of customer consumption. The City continued to evaluate meter performance and validate data quality for the annual AWWA water audit.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: During FY 2023-24, the City of Coalinga initiated its meter replacement program to improve customer metering accuracy and data reliability. The City began planning and procurement for new cellular read meters and developed an implementation schedule prioritizing the oldest or least accurate meters. Staff training and system integration work also began to ensure seamless transition to the new Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) platform.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Cal Water implemented leakage recovery pilots evaluating the effectiveness of satellite and manual acoustic leak detection. They also developed a master production meter inventory to document and help track production meter data across various databases.

They also developed a production database to digitally archive approved monthly production data across all districts in a centralized database. In addition, Cal Water has developed tools to allow for more frequent water loss tracking, including a Tableau visualization of monthly production and consumption data as well as quarterly water loss pulse checks. These tools allow Cal Water to flag potentially unrealistic water audit inputs and/or results for further investigation.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Cal Water implemented leakage recovery pilots evaluating the effectiveness of satellite and manual acoustic leak detection. The pilots were implemented in 4 systems with varying characteristics and geographic location. STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Cal Water conducted training on production data reporting, including the development of reference videos and documents to improve the data collection, management, and quality control of production data. They also developed a production database to digitally archive approved monthly production data across all districts in a centralized database. In addition, Cal Water has developed tools to allow for more frequent water loss tracking, including a Tableau visualization of monthly production and consumption data as well as quarterly water loss pulse checks. These tools allow Cal Water to flag potentially unrealistic water audit inputs and/or results for further investigation.

STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Continued implementation of a risk-based Customer Meter Asset Management Plan which addresses replacement and testing of demand meters, in order to enhance revenue protection and reduce apparent loss. Began acoustic leak detection to identify non-surfaced mainline leaks and reduce real water loss. Continued to use data from demand meters and updated orthophotography to refine SmartWorks, a software program which helps the District identify malfunctioning meters. This improves Rancho Water's ability to remotely detect apparent water loss, avoid lost revenue, and identify malfunctioning/stuck meters that require replacement.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: Continued revising production and demand meter calibration and testing policy, specifically implementing more frequent field testing. This work culminated with the development of separate production meter and demand meter calibration and testing programs.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Started pilot testing program for selected demand and production meters.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Continued implementation of the District's strategic approach to water loss reduction. This which centers on a comprehensive asset management program that combines: 1. Proactive infrastructure maintenance: prioritized pipeline and valve replacements to prevent potential leaks and infrastructure failures; completed corrosion survey of high-priority pipelines to indentify vulnerable pipeline sections; continued implementation of risk-based Customer Meter Asset Management Plan which addresses replacement of high demand meters; continued to use data from demand meters and updated orthophography to refine SmartWorks, a software program which helps the District identify malfunctioning meters. 2. Targeted leak detection: conducted enhanced acoustic leak detection guided by integrated satellite-based data; expanded the use of correlators to pinpoint leaks; initiated monitoring following mainline leaks repairs to promptly address leaks from repressurized pipes. 3. Targeted interventions: Focused on pipelines in vulnerable areas of the distribution system, reducing leak response times, minimizing water loss and infrastructure damage.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: Enhanced leak detection by integrating data from both satellite-based leak detection and traditional acoustic leak detection methods. Prioritized pipelines as part of pipeline asset management program. Selected high-risk pipelines for in-pipe leak detection and high-priority pipelines for corrosion survey. Revised CRUC calculations by applying volume-weighted average acrossall biling rates to align with AWWA tool requirements. Previously, the CRUC was calculatted using simple average.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: 2026: Developed a formal pipeline renewal program, committing $5 million annually over the next five years to replace aging potable water pipelines. In parallel, the District developed AI-aided risk and likelihood-of-failure models to identify high-risk areas of the distribution system and prioritize monitoring and leak detection activities. Leak detection program was expanded by deploying newly purchased acoustic loggers in areas with historically high main break rates. Installation of the remaining loggers is ongoing and will further support an expanded, risk-based leak detection program focused on proactive monitoring of the most vulnerable portions of the system. Increasing rate of customer meter replacement with emphasis on high-volume/revenue meters. Additionally, District implemented process improvements to enhance audit accuracy and cross-departmental coordination, to include: alignment with finalized net accrual values, expanded cross-functional review.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: 2025: District replaced 786 customer meters and continued replacing propeller flow production meters with more reliable electromagnetic meters. Improved water accounting practices by refining the calculation of volume from own source, exported and imported water, transitioning from report-based processed data to direct SCADA-derived data; similarly used Cayenta data for billed consumption rather than Sales Report. This improves accuracy and reliability of two main inputs to the audit software.Also, continued to address real loss by monitoring pipelines in neighborhoods with historic high break rate and ongong implementation of our valve replacement program

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: 2025 - San Gabriel Valley Water Company's- Fontana Division (Fontana) strives to improve data collection for assessing and reducing water losses while performing proactive measures to minimize real losses. Fontana field personnel are trained to spot leaks and verify if water from fire hydrants is metered, permitted, or if the water is taken without authorization. Additionally, all Fontana customers have been identified and are billed accordingly. To enhance measurement accuracy, Fontana is transitioning from using positive displacement meters to superior ultrasonic AMP meters for all its meters. These advanced meters excel at capturing low-flow usage. To date, roughly 7,800 meters have been replaced, and Fontana's goal is to maintain a pace of about 5,000 replacements per year until full conversion is achieved. Each meter will then follow a 15-year replacement cycle. Fontana also replaces all meters from 1.5-inch up to 6-inch when they reach 6 MG of consumption. Fontana tests all large meters 4-inch and above on an annual basis. Fontana retains records for each meter owned and used. As part of its ongoing efforts to improve system accuracy and reduce water loss, Fontana has implemented a new standard requiring the installation of ultrasonic meters on all new fire service connections that include on-site private fire hydrants. Lastly, in coordination with a 3rd party consultant, Fontana is preparing new procedures and practices to further reduce water loss and improve its reporting and score.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: 2024 - This water loss audit report meets the requirements of California Code of Regulations Title 23, Division 2, Chapter 7 and the California Water Code Section 10608.34 and has been prepared in accordance with the method adopted by the American Water Works Association, as contained in their manual, Water Audits and Loss Control Programs, Manual M36, Fourth Edition and in the Free Water Audit Software. In 2024, Fontana installed approximately 6,800 new ultrasonic AMR meters and continued installing check valves under any damaged fire hydrants. Fontana employs technologies including leak noise correlators and loggers and repaired 215 leaks. Fontana conducts various data analysis including production with sales comparison, AMR data analysis and reporting for leaks or high use customers, visual inspection by field personnel, customer and outside agency notice and reporting, immediate response to leak repairs, and ongoing valve and fire hydrant maintenance. Fontana also utilized 3rd party consulting services to identify areas of improvements to its Annual Water Loss report and score. Fontana completed the installation of a dedicated meter test bench. The test bench is used throughout the year to conduct meter audits, verify the accuracy of meters suspected of under- or over-registration, and support customer billing inquiries by providing documented meter accuracy results.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: 2023 - Fontana installed about 6,305 new ultrasonic AMR meters. Fontana installed check valves under any damaged fire hydrants. Fontana employs technologies including leak noise correlators and loggers and repaired 85 leaks. Fontana conducts production with sales comparison, visual inspection by field personnel, customer and outside agency notice and reporting, immediate response to leak repairs, and ongoing valve and fire hydrant maintenance.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Cal Water implemented leakage recovery pilots evaluating the effectiveness of satellite and manual acoustic leak detection. The pilots were implemented in 4 systems with varying characteristics and geographic location. In addition, Cal Water conducted a detailed investigation of repair data to calculate reported leakage volume and calculated the optimal leak detection survey frequency per the AWWA Manual M36 methodology. They also developed a master production meter inventory to document and help track production meter data across various databases.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Cal Water conducted training on production data reporting, including the development of reference videos and documents to improve the data collection, management, and quality control of production data. They also developed a production database to digitally archive approved monthly production data across all districts in a centralized database. In addition, Cal Water has developed tools to allow for more frequent water loss tracking, including a Tableau visualization of monthly production and consumption data as well as quarterly water loss pulse checks. These tools allow Cal Water to flag potentially unrealistic water audit inputs and/or results for further investigation.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Cal Water implemented leakage recovery pilots evaluating the effectiveness of satellite and manual acoustic leak detection. The pilots were implemented in 4 systems with varying characteristics and geographic location. In addition, Cal Water conducted a detailed investigation of repair data to calculate reported leakage volume and calculated the optimal leak detection survey frequency per the AWWA Manual M36 methodology. They also developed a master production meter inventory to document and help track production meter data across various databases.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Cal Water conducted training on production data reporting, including the development of reference videos and documents to improve the data collection, management, and quality control of production data. They also developed a production database to digitally archive approved monthly production data across all districts in a centralized database. In addition, Cal Water has developed tools to allow for more frequent water loss tracking, including a Tableau visualization of monthly production and consumption data as well as quarterly water loss pulse checks. These tools allow Cal Water to flag potentially unrealistic water audit inputs and/or results for further investigation.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: To support proactive leak detection, Cal Water designed a Leakage Recovery Pilot Plan to evaluate various leak detection technologies, including: Manual Acoustic Leak Detection Survey; Satellite & Aerial Imagery Analysis, Acoustic Logger Installation, and District Metered Area Monitoring

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: The water system's SCADA system automatically tracks levels in the City's 75,000-gallon and 1 MG storage tanks. For the upcoming 2023 audit, the City will track daily changes of stored water volumes in storage tanks and include the tabulation of the daily VOS quantity.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Electronic calibration was conducted on all groundwater supply wells, and supporting documentation of the electronic calibration was provided for the 2022 water audit.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: The City's meter replacment program consists of replacing at least 10% of the meter population on an annual basis to radio read meters. The meter replacment program will last for 10 years and will then start over. The City's billing department also monitors zero read meters and provides a list to water operators to test or replace on a monthly basis. Approximately 10 to 30 meters are replaced on a monthly basis by this process.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: The City will document daily fluctuations in stored water volumes and provide a comprehensive record of the daily Volume of Storage (VOS) data.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: The City continues to replace customer meters based on their age and specific circumstances, such as instances where a meter is malfunctioning or not working properly.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: Electronic calibration was performed on all groundwater supply wells on an annual basis, with supporting documentation submitted as part of the water audit validation.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: The City continued its customer meter replacement efforts and maintained reactive testing of malfunctioning meters. In 2025, the City began soliciting proposals for electronic calibration of the groundwater supply meters, with calibration activities scheduled to commence in 2026. Beginning in 2026, the City will perform electronic calibration of these meters on at least a semi-annual basis to ensure accurate source metering and improved data reliability.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: During the audit period, the City continued its ongoing meter replacement program, which replaces more than 300 meters per year, approximately 10 percent of the total meter population. The program targets all meters older than ten years to ensure accurate registration, reduce apparent losses, and maintain overall system reliability.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: The City initiated recording the Volume of Storage (VOS) data to better track fluctuations in system storage. Public Works staff also continued to test malfunctioning meters on a reactive basis as issues were identified.

In addition, Cal Water has developed tools to allow for more frequent water loss tracking, including a Tableau visualization of monthly production and consumption data as well as quarterly water loss pulse checks. These tools allow Cal Water to flag potentially unrealistic water audit inputs and/or results for further investigation.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: In the year after the audit year (2023), the City will enforce its water conservation measures through code compliance and will conduct follow-ups with customers identified as wasting water. Additionally, the City will continue replacing zero-read meters and those exhibiting anomalies to improve measurement accuracy and system efficiency.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: During the 2022 audit data year, the City took proactive steps to reduce both real and apparent water losses by systematically replacing customer meters that registered zero consumption or displayed irregularities. These efforts were aimed at improving the accuracy of customer billing data (apparent loss reduction) and ensuring that all water usage was being properly recorded. In addition, the City identifed potential service line issues and improved leak detection efforts, which contributed to the reduction of real losses in the distribution system.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: In the year preceding the audit data year (2021), the City undertook electronic calibration of its groundwater production meters to improve the precision of source water measurement. This initiative, coupled with the ongoing replacement of failed or zero-read customer meters, significantly enhanced the accuracy and reliability of both production and consumption data. Together, these actions strengthened the validity of the City's water data, supported more accurate water balance calculations, and contributed to more effective identification and tracking of water losses throughout the system.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: For the 2024 audit data year, the City will implement electronic calibration for groundwater production meters to enhance accuracy. Additionally, the City is assessing the feasibility of a citywide meter replacement program to transition all meters to Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI). Currently, the City's meter inventory consists of 25% radio-read meters and 75% manual-read meters. Beginning in 2024, the City will require developers to install AMI meters in all new developments to support this transition.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: In the 2023 audit year, the City enforced its water conservation measures through code compliance and conducted follow-ups with customers identified as wasting water. Additionally, the City continued replacing zero-read meters and those exhibiting anomalies to improve measurement accuracy and system efficiency.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: Prior to the 2023 audit year, the City proactively replaced zero-read meters and meters displaying anomalies to enhance water usage tracking and system reliability.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: 2025 – The City conducted flow-accuracy testing on all active groundwater wells. The City intends to perform this testing on an annual basis, or at a minimum on a semi-annual basis, to verify production measurement accuracy and support ongoing data reliability improvements.

In addition, the City began requiring installation of Advanced Metering Infrastructure (AMI) meters for all new developments to support the City's transition to automated metering and improved consumption data accuracy.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: 2023 – The City enforced its water conservation measures through code compliance activities and conducted follow-up actions with customers identified as wasting water. The City also continued replacing zero-read meters and meters exhibiting anomalous behavior to improve customer-meter accuracy and overall system efficiency.

They also developed a master production meter inventory to document and help track production meter data across various databases.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Cal Water conducted training on production data reporting, including the development of reference videos and documents to improve the data collection, management, and quality control of production data. In addition, Cal Water has developed tools to allow for more frequent water loss tracking, including a Tableau visualization of monthly production and consumption data as well as quarterly water loss pulse checks. These tools allow Cal Water to flag potentially unrealistic water audit inputs and/or results for further investigation.

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Cal Water implemented leakage recovery pilots evaluating the effectiveness of satellite and manual acoustic leak detection. The pilots were implemented in 4 systems with varying characteristics and geographic location. In addition, Cal Water conducted a detailed investigation of repair data to calculate reported leakage volume and calculated the optimal leak detection survey frequency per the AWWA Manual M36 methodology. They also developed a master production meter inventory to document and help track production meter data across various databases.
STEPS_YR_DURING_NOTES: Cal Water conducted training on production data reporting, including the development of reference videos and documents to improve the data collection, management, and quality control of production data. They also developed a production database to digitally archive approved monthly production data across all districts in a centralized database. In addition, Cal Water has developed tools to allow for more frequent water loss tracking, including a Tableau visualization of monthly production and consumption data as well as quarterly water loss pulse checks. These tools allow Cal Water to flag potentially unrealistic water audit inputs and/or results for further investigation.
STEPS_YR_BEFORE_NOTES: To support proactive leak detection, Cal Water designed a Leakage Recovery Pilot Plan to evaluate various leak detection technologies, including: Manual Acoustic Leak Detection Survey; Satellite & Aerial Imagery Analysis, Acoustic Logger Installation, and District Metered Area Monitoring

STEPS_YR_AFTER_NOTES: Cal Water expanded the leakage recovery pilots to 4 additional systems and added acoustic loggers to the technologies piloted. For Cal Water's small systems with less than 3,000 connections, a billing data analysis was performed and supply system schematics were developed to visualize the flow meters used to quantify water supplied volumes. In addition, Cal Water updated their Water Loss Control Plan, documenting the goals of the water loss program, achievements to date, and future improvements.
